text: I’ll first inspect the supplied STEP’s declared units and import it with OCCT, then report its topological contents and validity before choosing an extraction or meshing method.

The import is a valid three-solid assembly about 54 × 46 × 31 in its native coordinates. I’ll now inspect each solid and the complete STEP unit section; this distinguishes enclosure parts from any pre-existing internal volume and fixes the required metre scale.

No single-line unit record was found because STEP entities can split the unit definition across linked records. I’ll resolve the header/context records directly and render the three solids in distinct colors to understand how they form the flow enclosure.

The STEP context declares metres, while OCCT has converted the imported geometry to its millimetre working convention (the 53.95 native extent corresponds to 0.05395 m). I will therefore scale by 0.001 exactly once for export. The assembly appears to be three stacked enclosure pieces; I’ll inspect them separately and in section to identify the connected internal cavity and its openings rather than treating the part solids themselves as fluid.

The solids are not thin wall bodies: the central body occupies about 96% of its bounding box, and the upper piece is a bellmouth-like solid. That strongly suggests the STEP may already contain a partitioned fluid-domain assembly rather than physical casing walls. I’ll test whether the three solids overlap/touch into one connected volume and quantify the interfaces before deciding; this avoids inventing a cavity that the CAD does not contain.
The first interface test hit an empty Boolean result and therefore did not become part of the reproducible build. I’ll repeat it with explicit empty-result handling.

The three bodies do not overlap volumetrically, and the fuse still has two disconnected solids, so they are not a clean pre-partitioned fluid volume. I’ll now inspect a central cutaway of the actual material bodies to locate enclosed voids and the top/side openings; extraction will follow the cavity, not the nearly touching part interfaces.

The cutaway confirms there is no hollow core inside the blue body: it is the central flow-space solid itself, with adjoining upper and lower flow pieces. Thus the supplied “assembly” is a three-body representation of the fluid space, but its interfaces contain CAD tolerances that prevent a clean fuse. I’ll inspect STEP product/shape names and exact closest distances to determine intended connectivity and identify which external end faces are inlet/outlet.

The CAD names the parts `BASE`, `EMITTER`, and `BODY`, and every imported item is already a closed solid. Before treating their material as air, I’ll perform a cavity diagnostic: subtract the complete assembly from a surrounding test box and count disconnected void components. A genuine sealed internal air cavity would appear as an additional component; an open duct would still require identifiable boundary loops, which the closed solids do not have.

The complement has only the exterior component, so there is no sealed cavity. I’ll check each closed shell’s Euler characteristic next: a through-passage or open-ended bore in a solid changes the shell genus, whereas genus zero confirms these are simply connected material/shape solids without a duct running through them.

The supplied STEP does not contain the requested flow passage. OCCT imports three valid, closed solids (`LD19_BASE`, `LD19_EMITTER`, `LD19_BODY`), not enclosure shells around an internal volume. The surrounding-volume subtraction yields only one exterior component, and the terminal faces are closed material faces rather than inlet/outlet openings. Treating these solids themselves as air, or inventing an external domain and arbitrary inlet/outlet, would redesign the handed-off CAD.

No fluid solid was extracted, no fillets were altered, and no mesh was created. The STEP declares metres; OCCT imports its approximately 53.95 mm overall extent in native millimetres. A revised CAD containing the enclosure’s internal passage, or explicit identification of intended openings/domain, is required.
